# Animal sizes data
![](/images/blue_whale.png){style="width:200px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

For our scatter plot from real data we will look at the sizes of the largest animals in the world. This data is from: <https://en.Wikipedia.org/wiki/Largest_organisms>

The data contains the following information:

- Animal names
- Average mass in tonnes
- Maximum mass in tonnes
- Average total length in metres
- Group, in this case whether are they Mammals or Reptiles
- Biom, are they aquatic, semiaquatic, or terrestrial

Download the [animal_sizes.csv](https://neof-workshops.github.io/R_j4c0xh/downloads/animal_sizes.csv) file into your "plots" directory.

## Read in animal data
![](/images/reading_glasses.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

Next, __read__ the data into R. We have included a new option: `stringsAsFactors = TRUE`. This is important for plotting and will be explained more later.

```{r eval=FALSE}
animal_df <- read.csv("animal_sizes.csv", 
                      row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE,
                      stringsAsFactors = TRUE
                      )
``` 

## Average mass and max mass
![](/images/hippo.png){style="width:150px; background:white; border-radius:5px" fig-align="center"}

Check the column names with the __function__ `colnames()`. With these column names we can create some quick plots.

```{r, eval=FALSE}
colnames(animal_df)
```

Compare the average and maximum weight with a scatter plot.
```{r eval=FALSE}
plot(x = animal_df$`Average mass (tonnes)`,
     y = animal_df$`Maximum mass (tonnes)`)
``` 

Average and maximum weight appear to correlate as expected.

Sometimes a quick and easy plot is all you want. If you're not going to present a plot then it doesn't need to be pretty. 
As long as it is functional it is useful.
